name: Detox / slimming teas

lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal blends marketed for cleansing and weight loss, and many rely on senna, a plant whose sennosides are a stimulant laxative. Users drink them to de-bloat and look flatter around the stomach for a short window, such as before an event or photos.

Senna increases fluid and electrolytes in the large bowel and stimulates gut movement, so the scale change largely reflects stool and water loss rather than body fat. A 2015 review of detox diets found no compelling evidence for weight management or toxin elimination, and weight lost on such regimens is typically regained.

paras: People brew the tea for a few days, often timed to an event. It is usually combined with lighter eating during that period.

Reported senna effects are abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea and flatulence, and lower potassium, which can increase digoxin toxicity. Regular use can cause melanosis coli, a brown discoloration of the colon wall. Senna is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and some inflammatory bowel conditions.

angle.text: Users drink detox and slimming teas to de-bloat and drop scale weight quickly before events or photos. The change is typically fluid and gut contents rather than fat, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.

lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal beverages sold to cleanse the body of toxins or aid weight loss; many contain senna, an anthraquinone plant laxative. [1][2]

Detox diets in general claim to remove toxins through restricted intake or purging. A 2015 review concluded there was no compelling evidence supporting detox diets for weight management or toxin elimination. [1] Senna glycosides are an established stimulant laxative used for constipation and bowel preparation. [2]
infobox: Varies; senna is OTC laxative in the US

paras: Detox regimens claim that toxins stored in fat are released and eliminated through skin, urine, feces or breath; scientists and dietitians quoted by Wikipedia dispute this and note that the liver and kidneys already handle elimination. [1] Teas marketed in this category frequently include senna as the active laxative component. [2]

Senna glycosides are dimeric anthraquinones thought to raise fluid and electrolyte content in the large bowel and stimulate peristalsis; oral doses typically act within 6 to 12 hours. [2] Laxatives act after nutrient absorption in the small intestine, so effects on weight are mainly water loss. [3]

Reported effects of senna include abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence and discoloured urine; regular use can cause melanosis coli, and senna may increase digoxin toxicity by lowering potassium. Contraindications include intestinal obstruction, acute inflammatory bowel conditions and appendicitis. [2] Wikipedia notes older concerns about colon damage and dependence are no longer supported by current evidence, although high-quality long-term data are lacking. [2]
Wikipedia's laxative article reports that misuse can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances that can be potentially fatal. [3]
No studies found on slimming teas as a product category. A 2015 review of detox diets and the evidence on senna are described above. [1][2]
